transcript: Doctor: Good afternoon Mr. Patel, I'm Dr. Rivera. Your primary care physician referred you for right knee pain. Tell me what's been going on. Patient: It started about six months ago, just a dull ache after playing basketball. But it's gotten progressively worse. Now it hurts going up and down stairs and sometimes it swells after I've been on my feet all day. Doctor: Any locking or giving way of the knee? Patient: It catches sometimes, like something is blocking it from fully straightening. No giving way though. Doctor: Any previous injuries to this knee? Patient: I twisted it in college playing soccer maybe fifteen years ago but it got better on its own. I never had it looked at. Doctor: Alright let me examine you. I see mild effusion on the right compared to left. Range of motion is zero to one twenty, there's a positive McMurray test with a click on the medial side. Anterior drawer is stable, no varus or valgus laxity. Patient: What does that mean? Doctor: The McMurray test suggests a possible medial meniscus tear, likely degenerative given your age and history. The good news is your ligaments are intact. I'd like to get an MRI to confirm. In the meantime, I'm going to start you on an anti-inflammatory, recommend icing after activity, and refer you to physical therapy. Patient: Would I need surgery? Doctor: Let's see the MRI first. Many meniscus tears respond well to conservative treatment. If there's a significant bucket handle tear or mechanical symptoms persist, we'd discuss arthroscopic options. I'll have my scheduler set up the MRI this week. Patient: Thank you doctor, I appreciate you explaining everything.
